subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Dunning-Kruger Trap
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Dunning-Kruger Trap.

hook.text: A bank robber covered his face with lemon juice, sure cameras could not see him. He was genuinely shocked.

buildup.text: Dunning and Kruger tested people on logic and grammar. The worst performers rated themselves near the top.

discovery.text: Low skill prevents you from recognizing low skill. You need competence to even judge competence.

twist.text: High performers underestimate themselves. They assume their ease means the task is easy for everyone.

climax.text: To escape the trap, seek expert feedback early. You cannot self-assess in domains where you lack skill.

punchline.text: The less you know, the less you know you don't know.

quiz.question: What did Dunning and Kruger find about low performers?
options: They rated themselves near the top despite poor results
They refused to participate in the study

details.summary: The Dunning-Kruger trap in decision-making occurs when overconfident decision-makers take on challenges beyond their competence because they cannot accurately assess what they do not know. Their limited knowledge prevents them from recognizing the complexity they face.
details.whyItMatters: The Dunning-Kruger trap leads to under-preparation, inadequate risk assessment, and rejection of expert advice. Decision-makers who do not know what they do not know make bold moves in domains where caution is warranted.
takeaways: Overconfident beginners underestimate complexity and take excessive risks
The trap strengthens when feedback is delayed or ambiguous
Seeking contrary expert opinion is the best defense against overconfident decisions

faq.question: How does the Dunning-Kruger trap manifest in business decisions?
faq.answer: Entrepreneurs with surface knowledge enter complex markets confidently, managers make technology decisions without technical understanding, and investors choose strategies based on incomplete knowledge. Each feels competent precisely because they cannot see what they are missing.

faq.question: How can someone recognize they are in a Dunning-Kruger trap?
faq.answer: If you feel very confident about a domain you recently entered, that confidence itself is a warning sign. Seek the judgment of acknowledged experts. If experts are much more cautious than you, your confidence likely exceeds your competence.
